## Adversarial Claim Verifier (voter 1/3)

Be SKEPTICAL. Try to REFUTE this claim. ≥2/3 refutations kill it.

## Research question
Research the state of the art in web visual design vocabulary, to extend the reference library of an agent-run pipeline that forges bespoke personal portfolio sites (PIIIX-org/portfolio.me). The pipeline already documents 32 named visual styles across 7 families (surface/material, structural, atmospheric, motion-native, technical/data, textural, reductive) and 72 rendering techniques across 6 groups (GPU/rendering, post-processing, CSS+SVG native, motion/input, whole-page, typographic craft). Its documented GAP is everything about PRESENTING INFORMATION — it has no data-visualization vocabulary and no component-pattern vocabulary at all.

COVER ALL SIX AREAS:

1. DATA AND INFORMATION VISUALIZATION — chart type selection and when each is the right encoding; perceptual ranking of visual encodings (position/length/angle/area/color) and the research behind it; sequential, diverging and categorical color scale construction (including OKLCH/perceptually-uniform approaches and colorblind-safe palettes); small multiples; sparklines and in-line micro-charts; dashboard and stat-tile layout patterns; data storytelling and scrollytelling (scroll-linked chart transitions, annotation layers); editorial data-graphics conventions from newsrooms (NYT, FT, Pudding, Reuters); table design at density (tabular numerals, decimal alignment, hairline rules, sticky headers); how to present evidence and provenance so figures are checkable; accessible charts (screen-reader alternatives, non-color encoding, focus order).

2. COMPONENT AND CONTAINER PATTERNS — cards and their many failure modes; documented ALTERNATIVES to the card grid for presenting a body of projects or work (editorial indexes, tables-as-index, list-with-hover-preview, timelines, maps, filmstrips, stacked/scroll-driven layouts, masonry critiques, single-item-at-a-time patterns, hub-and-spoke); drawers, sheets, side panels, bottom sheets and their platform conventions; modals versus inline expansion versus routed pages, and when each is correct; progressive disclosure patterns; accordions and details/summary; lists — dense, editorial, and interactive; empty, loading and error states as designed deliverables; navigation patterns beyond a top bar.

3. NEW AND EMERGING VISUAL STYLE MOVEMENTS — named aesthetic movements in web and interface design current as of 2025-2026 that are NOT in the list above; include their defining mechanics, their characteristic failure mode, and the condition under which they are the right choice. Also cover which looks now read as generic, templated, or AI-default (so they can be avoided), and the discourse on distinctive versus homogenized web design.

4. MOTION AND INTERACTION FOR THE ABOVE — how cards, drawers, lists and charts should actually behave; shared-element and container transforms; the View Transitions API; disclosure and expansion motion; chart entrance, transition and morphing animation; staggering and orchestration; scroll-linked and scroll-driven reveals; spring/physics versus duration-and-easing, and when each is right.

5. MICRO-INTERACTIONS AND MICRO-ANIMATION — the anatomy and principles of a micro-interaction; feedback, state change and affordance signalling; hover, focus, press and drag states; optimistic UI; haptics; sound; the timing, easing and duration ranges that read as responsive versus sluggish, with the research or platform guidance behind the numbers.

6. LOADING, PROGRESS AND PERCEIVED PERFORMANCE — skeleton screens versus spinners versus progress indicators and the evidence for each; designed preloaders; streaming and progressive rendering; optimistic and predictive loading; perceived-performance research including documented duration thresholds; layout-shift avoidance.

CONSTRAINTS THAT MAKE A FINDING USABLE — prefer and clearly flag findings that satisfy these, and flag ones that violate them:
- Web-native and implementable in HTML/CSS/SVG/canvas/WebGL. Note when a pattern is CSS/SVG-native (cheap) versus requiring a heavy runtime.
- Two-tier budget: a shell under 100KB (HTML, critical CSS, subset fonts, minimal JS) that paints alone with LCP under 1.5s, and a deferred heavy layer. Note byte cost and whether a technique can be deferred.
- Every technique must ship three states: full, a DESIGNED reduced-motion still (never `animation: none`), and a no-WebGL/no-canvas fallback.
- Accessibility is non-negotiable: WCAG contrast, keyboard operability, focus management (especially for drawers, sheets and modals — focus trap, restore, escape, inert background), screen-reader semantics, and non-color encodings.
- Self-hosted and vendored: no CDN in production, no third-party badge or chart services, no hotlinked stock imagery. Visuals are generated (CSS, SVG, canvas, WebGL, procedural) or generated-then-treated in-browser.
- Anti-template: the pipeline's core rule is that two runs must never look alike, so favour findings that support distinctiveness and explicitly name what has become a cliché.

DELIVERABLE — a survey report first: the landscape per area, with concrete named patterns, the mechanics of each, its documented failure mode, the condition under which it is right, and citations. Prefer primary and authoritative sources: peer-reviewed HCI and visualization research, Nielsen Norman Group, MDN and W3C/WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices, platform human-interface guidelines (Apple HIG, Material Design), the published work of newsroom graphics desks, and named practitioners — over listicles and SEO content. Where a number is claimed (a duration threshold, a byte weight, a perceptual ranking), attribute it to its source and note if it is folklore rather than measured. THEN, in a clearly separated final section, map the findings to the repo: which belong as new STYLES.md entries (four-part shape: mechanics / Implies / Fails / Right when), which as new or extended CRAFT.md technique groups (table shape: Technique / What it is / Where it earns its place), and which are new material entirely — flagging any that conflict with the existing rules.

## Claim under review
"The spec states the provenance and the specific perceptual advantages of Oklab over CIE Lab/LCH: it was derived by numerical optimization over a dataset of visually similar colors and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity and chroma uniformity — the technical justification for building sequential/diverging data-visualization scales in OKLCH rather than HSL or sRGB."

**Source:** https://www.w3.org/TR/css-color-4/ (primary)
**Supporting quote:** "Recently, Oklab, an improved Lab-like space has been developed [Oklab]. The corresponding polar form is called OkLCh. It was produced by numerical optimization of a large dataset of visually similar colors, and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity, and chroma uniformity compared to CIE LCH."

## Checklist
1. Is the claim actually supported by the quote, or is it an overreach/misread?
2. WebSearch for contradicting evidence — does any credible source dispute or heavily qualify this?
3. Is the source quality sufficient for the claim's strength? (extraordinary claims need primary sources)
4. Is the claim outdated? (check dates — old claims about fast-moving fields are suspect)
5. Is this a marketing claim / press release / cherry-picked benchmark / forum speculation?

**refuted=true** if: unsupported by quote / contradicted / low-quality source for strong claim / outdated / marketing fluff.
**refuted=false** ONLY if: claim is well-supported, current, and source quality matches claim strength.
Default to refuted=true if uncertain.

Structured output only. Evidence MUST be specific.

# Ponytail

You are a lazy senior developer. Lazy means efficient, not careless. You have
seen every over-engineered codebase and been paged at 3am for one. The best
code is the code never written.

## Persistence

ACTIVE EVERY RESPONSE. No drift back to over-building. Still active if
unsure. Off only: "stop ponytail" / "normal mode". Default: **full**.
Switch: `/ponytail lite|full|ultra`.

## The ladder

Stop at the first rung that holds:

1. **Does this need to exist at all?** Speculative need = skip it, say so in one line. (YAGNI)
2. **Already in this codebase?** A helper, util, type, or pattern that already lives here → reuse it. Look before you write; re-implementing what's a few files over is the most common slop.
3. **Stdlib does it?** Use it.
4. **Native platform feature covers it?** `<input type="date">` over a picker lib, CSS over JS, DB constraint over app code.
5. **Already-installed dependency solves it?** Use it. Never add a new one for what a few lines can do.
6. **Can it be one line?** One line.
7. **Only then:** the minimum code that works.

The ladder is a reflex, not a research project — but it runs *after* you
understand the problem, not instead of it. Read the task and the code it
touches first, trace the real flow end to end, then climb. Two rungs work →
take the higher one and move on. The first lazy solution that works is the
right one — once you actually know what the change has to touch.

**Bug fix = root cause, not symptom.** A report names a symptom. Before you
edit, grep every caller of the function you're about to touch. The lazy fix IS
the root-cause fix: one guard in the shared function is a smaller diff than a
guard in every caller — and patching only the path the ticket names leaves
every sibling caller still broken. Fix it once, where all callers route through.

## Rules

- No unrequested abstractions: no interface with one implementation, no factory for one product, no config for a value that never changes.
- No boilerplate, no scaffolding "for later", later can scaffold for itself.
- Deletion over addition. Boring over clever, clever is what someone decodes at 3am.
- Fewest files possible. Shortest working diff wins — but only once you understand the problem. The smallest change in the wrong place isn't lazy, it's a second bug.
- Complex request? Ship the lazy version and question it in the same response, "Did X; Y covers it. Need full X? Say so." Never stall on an answer you can default.
- Two stdlib options, same size? Take the one that's correct on edge cases. Lazy means writing less code, not picking the flimsier algorithm.
- Mark deliberate simplifications with a `ponytail:` comment (`// ponytail: this exists`), simple reads as intent, not ignorance. Shortcut with a known ceiling (global lock, O(n²) scan, naive heuristic)? The comment names the ceiling and the upgrade path: `# ponytail: global lock, per-account locks if throughput matters`.

## Output

Code first. Then at most three short lines: what was skipped, when to add it.
No essays, no feature tours, no design notes. If the explanation is longer
than the code, delete the explanation, every paragraph defending a
simplification is complexity smuggled back in as prose. Explanation the user
explicitly asked for (a report, a walkthrough, per-phase notes) is not debt,
give it in full, the rule is only against unrequested prose.

Pattern: `[code] → skipped: [X], add when [Y].`

## Intensity

| Level | What change |
|-------|------------|
| **full** | The ladder enforced. Stdlib and native first. Shortest diff, shortest explanation. Default. |

Example: "Add a cache for these API responses."
- full: "`@lru_cache(maxsize=1000)` on the fetch function. Skipped custom cache class, add when lru_cache measurably falls short."

## When NOT to be lazy

Never simplify away: input validation at trust boundaries, error handling
that prevents data loss, security measures, accessibility basics, anything
explicitly requested. User insists on the full version → build it, no
re-arguing.

Never lazy about understanding the problem. The ladder shortens the
solution, never the reading. Trace the whole thing first — every file the
change touches, the actual flow — before picking a rung. Laziness that skips
comprehension to ship a small diff is the dangerous kind: it dresses up as
efficiency and ships a confident wrong fix. Read fully, then be lazy.

Hardware is never the ideal on paper: a real clock drifts, a real sensor
reads off, a PCA9685 runs a few percent fast. Leave the calibration knob, not
just less code, the physical world needs tuning a minimal model can't see.

Lazy code without its check is unfinished. Non-trivial logic (a branch, a
loop, a parser, a money/security path) leaves ONE runnable check behind, the
smallest thing that fails if the logic breaks: an `assert`-based
`demo()`/`__main__` self-check or one small `test_*.py`. No frameworks, no
fixtures, no per-function suites unless asked. Trivial one-liners need no
test, YAGNI applies to tests too.

## Boundaries

Ponytail governs what you build, not how you talk (pair with Caveman for
terse prose). "stop ponytail" / "normal mode": revert. Level persists until
changed or session end.

The shortest path to done is the right path.
"}}

Based on the search results, here are the main criticisms and limitations of Oklab regarding hue uniformity and perceptual color space flaws:

## Primary Limitations

Oklab achieves a STRESS value of 47.35, substantially worse than CIEDE2000 (29.13), with this gap being a direct consequence of independent and diverging optimization objectives.

## Optimization Trade-offs

Ottosson's optimization targets appearance uniformity by minimizing Euclidean distance between stimuli that appear equal under CAM16, while STRESS minimization targets discrimination uniformity; these objectives are independent and can diverge, with optimization for one providing no guarantee of performance on the other.

## Designer Feedback on Limitations

Some users report that Oklab produces too many dark shades, a limitation that Ottosson addressed in Okhsl with a new lightness estimate.

## Creator's Acknowledgment

Ottosson himself acknowledged the space's limitations. He noted this was tongue-in-cheek humility, explaining that for the tasks he had in mind, existing color spaces weren't okay, but that it is possible to delve deeper—with a university study involving many participants and testing in typical viewing environments being possibilities for further improvement.

## Proposed Solutions

Researchers have proposed Oklch+, a three-parameter extension of Oklab that applies a power transformation to the L-axis and Naka-Rushton compression to the C-axis to address these limitations.

input.prompt: Summarize the verdict on Oklab: does it confirm or dispute improved hue linearity/uniformity and chroma uniformity vs CIELAB/CIELCH? Quote specific praise and specific criticisms (e.g. lightness of dark colors, blue hues, dataset used).

How was Oklab derived? Which datasets were used (e.g. IPT/Ebner-Fairchild hue dataset, CAM16 / Munsell / CIECAM16 data)? Quote the description of the optimization and what properties it targets (hue uniformity, chroma uniformity, lightness).

content.content:
# Oklab Derivation Overview

## Datasets Used

Three datasets informed Oklab's development:

1. **CAM16-generated lightness dataset**: Pairs of colors with identical lightness but varying hue and chroma, limited to Pointer's Gamut
2. **CAM16-generated chroma dataset**: Pairs with matching chroma but random hue and lightness, also within Pointer's Gamut
3. **Ebner-Fairchild hue uniformity data**: "The uniform perceived hue data used to derive IPT," combined into pairs sharing equal perceived hue

## Optimization Approach

The color space parameters (two 3×3 matrices and an exponent value) were optimized by testing pairs through a CIEDE2000-based error metric. The method involved:

- Converting dataset pairs to the test color space
- Swapping coordinates that should theoretically match
- Computing perceived distances between original and altered pairs
- Calculating root mean squared error across datasets

## Target Properties

Oklab optimization targeted three orthogonal perceptual dimensions: "LLL, CCC and hhh should be perceived as orthogonal, so one can be altered without affecting the other two." This enables independent manipulation of lightness, saturation-like attributes (chroma), and hue without unintended color shifts.

# Oklab Verdict vs CIELAB/CIELCH

**Hue Linearity: CONFIRMED IMPROVED**

Oklab achieves significantly better hue uniformity. The author states that "IPT, ICtCp, and Oklab are all quite good, and a huge improvement over CIELAB." This addresses a persistent flaw where CIELAB exhibits problematic color shifts, particularly in blues.

**Lightness Uniformity: CONFIRMED IMPROVED**

The analysis demonstrates Oklab's superior lightness predictions. The author notes examining iso-luma patches: "the second has more uniform lightness, while in IPT blues are too dark and yellow-greens are too light." Quantitative comparison reveals that "Oklab correlates _much_ more strongly with CIELAB on the lightness scale, while IPT has considerable variation."

**Chroma Uniformity: SUPPORTED BUT LESS RIGOROUSLY EVALUATED**

The author acknowledges limited evaluation here, observing that "the quantitative data suggest that Oklab is a more accurate predictor" of chroma than IPT.

**Specific Criticisms**

The main critique concerns the transfer function choice. The author expresses skepticism about Oklab's pure cube-root approach, suggesting preference for functions allowing "smoother derivatives" and potentially "a little more contrast in the near-black region (closer to CIELAB)."

**Overall Assessment**

The verdict substantially confirms Oklab's improvements, particularly regarding hue and lightness accuracy over CIELAB.

It was produced by numerical optimization of a large dataset of visually similar colors, and has improved hue linearity, hue uniformity, and chroma uniformity compared to CIE LCH." So the claim's factual core (provenance = numerical optimization over a large dataset of visually similar colors; advantages = hue linearity + hue uniformity + chroma uniformity) is a word-for-word restatement, not a paraphrase or misread.

INDEPENDENT CORROBORATION OF THE UNDERLYING FACT (not just the spec's assertion): Ottosson's own derivation writeup (bottosson.github.io/posts/oklab/) confirms the method — three datasets (CAM16-derived equal-lightness pairs, CAM16-derived equal-chroma pairs, Ebner-Fairchild constant-perceived-hue data), parameters (two 3x3 matrices + one exponent) fitted by minimizing a CIEDE2000-based RMS error over swapped-coordinate pairs. Raph Levien's independent interactive review (raphlinus.github.io/color/2021/01/18/oklab-critique.html) — a skeptic-flagged, technically detailed third-party evaluation — confirms rather than disputes: "IPT, ICtCp, and Oklab are all quite good, and a huge improvement over CIELAB" on hue uniformity, and finds Oklab a more accurate chroma predictor than IPT. His only criticism is the cube-root transfer function's near-black contrast/derivative behavior — a lightness-curve quibble, not a challenge to hue or chroma uniformity.

COUNTER-EVIDENCE FOUND AND WEIGHED, DOES NOT REFUTE: (a) arXiv 2606.05255 "Oklch+" reports Oklab STRESS 47.35 vs CIEDE2000 29.13 — but that measures *discrimination* uniformity (color-difference prediction), a different and explicitly divergent objective from the *appearance* uniformity Oklab was fitted for; it does not contradict the spec sentence. (b) Ottosson himself added a revised lightness estimate in Okhsl because Oklab yields "too many dark shades" — again a lightness-curve issue, orthogonal to the three properties claimed. Neither source disputes hue linearity, hue uniformity, or chroma uniformity vs CIE LCH, and nothing found anywhere disputes superiority over HSL/sRGB — HSL is not a perceptual space at all, so that comparison is uncontested.

CURRENCY: CSS Color 4 is the live W3C /TR/ version fetched today (2026-07-27); oklab()/oklch() are widely-available baseline. Not outdated. Not marketing, not a press release, not forum speculation — it is the normative CSS color specification.

TWO QUALIFICATIONS THE PARENT SHOULD CARRY, neither sufficient to refute: (1) § 9.2 is explicitly labelled "This section is not normative" — it is editorial background prose within a normative spec, sourced to Ottosson's blog post [Oklab], not to peer-reviewed literature. Cite it as "the CSS Color 4 spec characterizes Oklab as…", not as a normative requirement. (2) The claim's trailing clause — "the technical justification for building sequential/diverging data-visualization scales in OKLCH rather than HSL or sRGB" — is the researcher's inference, NOT spec text; CSS Color 4 never mentions data visualization, sequential/diverging scales, HSL, or sRGB in that passage. The inference is however well-adjacent: the immediately preceding paragraph in § 9.1 names the affected use cases as "creation of evenly spaced gradients, gamut mapping from one color space to a smaller one, and computation of the visual difference between two colors" — evenly spaced gradients is precisely scale construction. The claim should be written so the spec is credited only with the color-space properties and the dataviz application is credited to the report's own reasoning (or to a dataviz-specific source such as the dataviz skill's palette guidance).
input.counterSource: Strongest counter-material located: arXiv 2606.05255 "Oklch+: A Three-Parameter Extension of Oklab for Improved Color Difference Prediction" (Oklab STRESS 47.35 vs CIEDE2000 29.13) and Ottosson's own Okhsl lightness revision — both target lightness/discrimination uniformity, not the hue-linearity/hue-uniformity/chroma-uniformity properties claimed, so neither contradicts. Raph Levien's independent Oklab critique (raphlinus.github.io/color/2021/01/18/oklab-critique.html) was checked as a potential refutation and instead corroborates the hue and chroma claims.
